chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Polls, Who's Who and the power of the press
summary: Hodes says his name never appeared in the polls or in Who's Who for years. He recounts the Disneyland booking lost after a review and a bad DownBeat review.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well, I just name one. Don't you think it hurt Edmund Hall? Sure, Louis gave him some work and all that, but don't you think it hurts -- okay, take me. I look on the polls and I don't see my name on there, time after time after time. It never appears. And for the longest time, I wasn't even in the Who's Who in Jazz that was put out.
Who's Who? Well, Teo was putting it out.

It's only later that they figured the hatchet had been buried deep enough in my head, let it go and go ahead. But even when I was in California and sat across from him, and then when we left town the writeup followed us again. It was Jim Beebe that showed me the writeup, told me about it. That he was still after me. He says, you should read the writeup. He says, the band was the Chicagoans, and the only guy there that played anything good was the guy that wasn't from Chicago, Barney Bigard.

And he still had that little poke at the music. And so I didn't get back to Disneyland. I talked to that man, we were very close friends. And there was a good feeling between the man that booked us and me. But after that, I never reached him. I thought maybe he'd lost the job or something. This is what the press can do. They can hurt you very badly. You're

part of the press, you know that the power of the press -- for example, I have a friend who just died, Veria? Wilson. And he would talk about a certain musician, I won't name him, who was a bandleader, who has a son who takes care of the books. And every time he gets paid, there's money missing off his payroll.
And he says, I'd rather beat him with a sword in his hand than a pen.

And to me, that shows how mighty than pen is. You sit down and -- you could retract all you want. For example, this last DownBeat, the review of my book, Selections From the Gutter, that was totally -- the wrong guy reviewed it. It's not that it should be glorified, but at least it should be reviewed by somebody that doesn't hate that period in history or doesn't put it down, doesn't want to know anything about it. It should be somebody that could be fair about it, could remove himself and review it.
So the pen to me has always been mighty, and this puts the musician in a very dire spot, because he can't put the pen down because he might need him.
